newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan sees business gains in Afghan upset.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan sees business gains in Afghan upset.

text.p: Pakistan, accused of interference in the Afghan conflict, expects more of business than political gains from the latest twist of the turmoil there.

Pakistan seemed to have these gains in mind when it became the first country to signal recognition of the new Taleban government in Afghanistan on Friday, hours after the Islamic militia stormed into the capital Kabul, analysts said.

President Burhanuddin Rabbani's ousted government had been an obstacle to Islamabad's dream of opening overland trade routes to Central Asia via Afghanistan, while neighbouring Iran had already built a rail link to serve as a bridge between Central Asia and Europe.

Kabul blocked once-agreed Pakistani plans early this year to repair the war-damaged road and lay a railway line through the Taleban-controlled western Afghanistan to link up with the former Soviet Central Asian republics.
Proposals to use the route through the Rabbani-controlled parts of eastern and northern Afghanistan remained stalled by procedural disputes or factional fighting there.
But with a Taleban government in Kabul, Pakistan can hope to realise its trade dreams soon, according to traders.
"If peace is restored in Afghanistan...Pakistan will get a very big market in Afghanistan and Central Asia, the head of Pakistan's national organisation of traders said.

Ilyas Ahmad Bilour, president of the Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FPCCI) said he did not expect peace there in the near future, however. "If peace is restored, Pakistan will get the market with trade in local currency, which will be helpful to our country."
One of Pakistan's major economic plans held up by the Afghan conflict is to build gas and oil pipelines with the the Central Asian republic of Turkmenistan through Afghanistan.

Taleban's birth two years ago as a movement of Islamic theology students is linked with trade, which it wanted to promote despite its apparent preoccupation with the avowed aim of enforcing what it regards as a strict Islamic order.
The movement burst into prominence when it launched a campaign in southern Afghanistan in October 1994 to remove checkpoints set up by various factions on roads primarily to extort toll from traders.

The first suspicions of Pakistan's links with the Taleban were voiced when the militia rescued a Pakistani trail-blazing 30-truck trade convoy to Central Asia in November the same year, four days after it was blocked by two guerrilla warlords, and then went on to score its major victory by capturing the former royal capital of Kandahar.
Many of Taleban's members have studied in Pakistani religious madrassahs, or schools, run by fundamentalist Islamic groups.

One of Kabul's most vociferous protests about the alleged Pakistani involvement came in September last year when the Taleban took the main pro-government western town of Herat, capital of the province of the same name bordering Iran.

Pakistan has not reopened its embassy in Afghanistan since a mob expressed its anger over Herat's fall by burning Islamabad's mission in Kabul, killing an embassy employee and beating up the ambassador and other staff.
Pakistan said on Friday it would deal with the new government and would immediately send a delegation to establish contact with it.

Islamabad's move contrasted with general concern expressed elsewhere against the Taleban's summary execution of former Afghan president Najibullah, his brother Shahpur Ahmadzai and two aides after dragging them out of a United Nations compound where they had lived for protection four and a half years.

"The assassination would give an insight into the type of governance that could be expected from a faction which came into prominence only two years ago, and little is known of its political background," Pakistani newspaper The News commented on Saturday.

Many Pakistanis also fear Taleban's rule in Afghanistan could encourage fundamentalist groups in Pakistan, which have often engaged in violence -- either in fighting between rival sects or mounting political protests.
Pakistan says it has no favourites among the Afghan factions, some of whom it helped during their guerrilla war against Soviet occupation of their country in the 1980s.

Former Pakistan army chief Mirza Aslam Beg said Islamabad was never behind the Taleban, and added: "If they succeed in bringing a lasting peace to Afghanistan, it would bring prosperity to Pakistan as it would give us safe and shortest passage to Central Asia."
